problems.stem: A storyboard frame narrates an on-screen animation with a paragraph of printed text shown at the same time. Citing the dual-channel and limited-capacity assumptions of the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, which redesign is best justified?
options: Keep the printed paragraph and add a third caption track so every learner has options.
Move the explanation to spoken narration and delete the simultaneous printed paragraph so the visual channel is not overloaded by redundant text.
Make the printed paragraph larger and bold so it is easier to read alongside the animation.
Replace the animation with the same printed paragraph so only one channel is used.
problems.explanation: Both the animation and the printed text load the visual channel, so they compete for limited visual working memory. Narrating the explanation routes it to the auditory channel, splitting the processing across both channels.

problems.stem: In Mayer's model, what must happen for information to move from sensory memory into working memory?
options: The learner must store it permanently in long-term memory first.
The learner must select relevant words and images through attention before the rest decays.
The system must present the same content in every modality simultaneously.
The information transfers automatically because sensory memory has unlimited duration.
problems.explanation: Sensory memory holds incoming material only briefly. The learner must actively select relevant words and images, or the material decays before it reaches the capacity-limited working memory.

problems.stem: A designer claims a screen is effective because it 'presents the content in both pictures and words.' Why is this not yet evidence of meaningful learning under the active-processing assumption?
options: Because pictures should never be paired with words in any design.
Because presenting in two formats does not by itself show the learner selected, organized, and integrated the material into a coherent mental model.
Because the screen needs more decorative graphics to engage learners.
Because all words should be spoken rather than printed in every case.
problems.explanation: The active-processing assumption says learning requires the learner to build verbal and pictorial models and integrate them. Dual presentation is a necessary condition, not proof that integration occurred.

problems.stem: A long, expert-written narration accompanies a complex diagram with many interacting parts. Two novices report feeling overwhelmed. Mapping this to the three memory stores, where is the bottleneck and what redesign follows?
options: The bottleneck is long-term memory; add a final summary slide to store everything.
The bottleneck is limited working-memory capacity processing many interacting elements at once; segment the diagram into parts the learner advances through and give pacing control.
The bottleneck is sensory memory; increase the font size of the narration transcript.
There is no bottleneck; novices simply need to watch the narration twice.
problems.explanation: Many interacting elements raise the load on capacity-limited working memory for novices who lack schemas. Segmenting and learner-paced advancement reduce the number of elements processed at once.

problems.stem: A teammate revises a storyboard frame: they cut the decorative stock photo, shorten the redundant printed paragraph, and also delete the 'predict what happens next' prompt because it 'slows learners down.' Load ratings drop and the teammate calls it a win. What did the revision get wrong?
options: Nothing; any change that lowers reported load is an improvement.
It removed germane processing: the prediction prompt was productive difficulty that builds the schema, not extraneous load to strip.
It should have kept the stock photo, because images always aid learning.
It lowered intrinsic load, which designers must never touch.
problems.explanation: The photo and redundant paragraph were extraneous load, so cutting them was right. But the prediction prompt provoked germane processing, the selecting, organizing, and integrating that builds the mental model. Deleting it trades away learning to lower felt effort: a germane-load casualty.
